input.question: Which educational institution did Károly Szakonyi attend?

documents.text: As Károly Szakonyi sat at his worn wooden desk, surrounded by stacks of dog-eared books and scattered papers, he stared out the window at the grey Budapest sky. His mind wandered back to the days when the sea air filled his lungs, and the sound of gulls crying overhead was his constant companion. It was a lifetime ago, yet the memories remained as vivid as the characters he brought to life on the page. He began to scribble notes in the margin of his manuscript, the words flowing effortlessly as he recalled the lectures of Professor Nakamura at Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology. The old man's passion for the ocean's secrets had been infectious, and Károly's own fascination with the mysteries beneath the waves had been ignited. He remembered the way the sunlight danced through the aquariums in the university's research facility, casting an ethereal glow over the bustling students. As he wrote, the characters in his story began to take shape. There was Emiko, the brilliant and introverted marine biologist, who had been his study partner and confidante during those long, sleepless nights in Tokyo. And then there was Captain József, the grizzled old sailor who had regaled them with tales of the open sea over steaming bowls of ramen in the university's cafeteria. Károly's thoughts were interrupted by the sound of his wife, Erzsébet, calling from the kitchen. "Károly, dear, would you like some coffee?" He smiled, his mind still half-lost in the world of his story. "Yes, thank you, my love. And perhaps some of those lovely Japanese biscuits you brought back from the market?" As he waited for Erzsébet to bring in the tray, Károly's gaze fell upon the small, framed photograph on his desk. It was a faded snapshot of himself and Emiko, taken on the deck of a research vessel in Tokyo Bay. They were both grinning from ear to ear, their faces wind-whipped and sun-kissed. He felt a pang of nostalgia, but it was tempered by the knowledge that those experiences had shaped him into the writer he was today. With a sense of renewed purpose, Károly turned back to his manuscript, the words flowing effortlessly as the characters of his story came alive once more.
